questions.title: The sodium-potassium pump is constantly active
questions.subject: fnd
questions.module_subject: SCU-FBS102 > Physiology > Cell Physiology > Membrane Transport
questions.question: Based on the fact that the Na+/K+-ATPase is a vital active transporter across the cell membrane, which of the following statements about it is true?

options.A: Sodium is actively transported exclusively into the cell
options.B: Potassium is actively transported exclusively out of the cell
options.C: An exactly equal number of sodium and potassium ions are transported each cycle
options.D: The pump is constantly active, continuously exchanging sodium and potassium

explanations.A: Incorrect. The Na+/K+-ATPase actively pumps sodium out of the cell, not into it; sodium moves into the cell passively down its gradient through leak channels and other transporters, not via this pump.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This reverses the pump's direction for potassium — the pump actively transports potassium into the cell, not out of it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The exchange is unequal: the pump moves three Na+ ions out for every two K+ ions it brings in per cycle, making it electrogenic rather than a one-for-one swap.
explanations.D: Correct. Because leak channels constantly allow some Na+ back into the cell and some K+ back out, the Na+/K+-ATPase must run continuously, not intermittently, in essentially every cell of the body, simply to maintain the resting ionic gradients against this ongoing leak. This baseline activity is a major consumer of the cell's ATP and is what maintains the negative resting membrane potential shared by virtually every cell.

questions.learning_objective: State that the Na+/K+-ATPase is continuously (not intermittently) active in nearly all cells, pumping 3 Na+ out for every 2 K+ in per cycle, to maintain resting ionic gradients against constant leak.
